The Southern method of securing that great boon, "a pure ballot," for which the Democratic platform pronounces in its second article, have been resumed in Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.

In Texas, Amos T. Bissell, a Union sailor, and now a revenue officer, made a temperate Republican speech to the negroes. But he complained that while ample provisions were made for the education of white children, only partial provision was made for colored; and that assessment for taxes was two or three times as much on the property of colored people as on the same kind of property belonging to white people; and, further, that while colored people confined in jail awaiting trial, were hired out for the benefit of the county treasury, white men in the same fix were not interfered with. He advised the colored people to strive to elevate and improve their condition. For this offence he was threatened with death by three distinct parties, and that with such details as terrified the man into giving up his situation under the Government, and flying to Galveston for safety. His enemies had the insolence to apply to the Galveston collector to secure his removal for the offence of making Republican speeches. We are glad to see that Attorney General Devens has taken the matter up, and orders an investigation. He is reported as saying that "If the courts of the National Government cannot protect the right of freedom of speech there will be no such tolerated in the South." But we greatly doubt the power of the United States Courts, as at present constructed, to secure that or any other right to the Southern Republicans. This is what could not be said of the courts of any other civilized nation.

In Mississippi, the brother of the murdered Col. Dixon visited Yazoo to attend the deathbed and funeral of the Colonel's widow, who has died of a broken heart. Mr. Dixon had the audacity to talk politics, and to predict the election of Garfield and Arthur. He was warned to leave Yazoo, and was told they would have no such talk there, nor any voting for Garfield.

South Carolina Bull-Dozers Under Orders.
CHARLESTON, S. C., July 24.—The first bingle-blast in the campaign to assemble the Republicans of Barnwell county at Blackville, on July 27, for the purpose of ratifying the nominations made at Chicago, has aroused the Democratic bull-dozen to action, and the kind of reception they will accord the Republicans can be conjectured from expressions in the Barnwell newspapers. The People says: "We learn that E. W. M. Mackey and W. N. Taft, the bravest and most brazen Radicals in the State, together with numerous lesser party lights, will be in Blackville on Tuesday. There is one lesson which the Republicans of this State have not yet learned. The sooner they know and become reconciled to the inevitable, the better it will be for them. It is this: The Democrats have obtained control of the State of South Carolina, and they intend to retain it at every hazard and in spite of the utmost efforts of local enemies and their Northern allies. We are requested by the highest competent Democratic authority to invite all Democratic candidates to attend the Republican meeting. They are expected to be on hand. The Barnwell Sentinel, after cutting the object of the meeting, says: "It is the duty of the Democratic party to have representatives at this meeting from all parts of the county. So let all clubs send fair representatives among them. Let them be men who will nail lies to the wall as fast as they are told. Democratic capsid candidates should attend to a man.

The clubs mentioned are the notorious Red Shirt, Rifle and Sabre Clubs which committed the outrage and murder in 1876 in Ellerton, only a few miles from Blackville, in the same county. They will, of course, attend the meeting, and, in accordance with their usual method, become masters of ceremony, invite Democratic speakers on the stand, and order the Republicans to step off, and if the latter do not choose to listen to the former they can go away. The result will be a Democratic "pow-wow." It would be an excellent opportunity for Northern Republicans to come to the meeting, unknown and unannounced, and witness the treat Republicans receive in this State who are brave enough to assert their manhood. Partially Excusable.
entertained by Republicans for Southern Democrats is partially excusable. They really are a most aggravating lot. Not content with voting the Democratic the perverse creatures persist in thwarting Republican designs in the most unbearable and disheartening manner.

Only a few days ago one of the most promising Republican schemes ever devised was brought to naught by these disobliging Democrats. There was a meeting of colored Republicans at Blackville, South Carolina; and as there were over four thousand present it was confidently hoped the Democrats of the vicinity would break up the meeting. Some of the more sanguine ventured to expect that a colored man or two would be shot; and even the gloomiest of Republican prophets predicted a case of rail-riding, and another of tar and feathers. Singularly enough the Democrats didn't come to the scratch. They were present in great numbers, but they obstinately persisted in listening attentively to what the speakers had to say, and in the most pusillanimous manner possible, refrained even from jeering. It was frightfully discouraging to the Republican organizers of the meeting. The speakers were prodded up to sharper abuse of the Democracy and their candidates, and the crowd roared its loudest for Garfield and Arthur. And there those despicable and aggravating Democrats stood all the time, without pulling a pistol or throwing an egg, or even interrupting a speaker. If they had only groaned it would have been something; for the Republicans could have flown to the telegraph office and dispatched the news north that their meeting had been broken up by a Democratic mob. But they wouldn't even groan. They absolutely had the brazen effrontery to stay through the entire meeting, until the speakers and hearres had howled themselves out of breath, without giving the faintest sign of disapproval.

No wonder the Republicans are discouraged when Democrats at the South act in so exceedingly unsatisfactory a manner. How in the name of all the Republican candidates at once is the Northern outrage market to be supplied if this thing is permitted to go on? The old-fashioned method—the Frances Thompson and Eliza Pinkston style—has been tried too often. It will not do any longer. The people want something fresh. They want an actual, blood-curdling, soul-harrowing outrage, with real martyrs, whose wrongs will stand examination and cross-examination. And how can they have this if the Southern Democracy ruthlessly refuses, as it did at Blackville, to play the part assigned it?—Detroit Free Press.

The Boston Herald, independent, calls Senator Conkling's late speech in New York "the speech of a partisan rather than a patriot—of an adversary rather than a statesman." "It is not such a speech as we were accustomed to hear from Daniel Webster, nor as the people flocked to hear from Henry Clay; but Mr. Conkling belongs to the new school of politicians—the men who 'boss' instead of lead; who dominate by the force of their personality and will, rather than by their intellect or the power of their ideas. A forceful speech is this New York effort, but, judged by any high standard, it cannot be called an eloquent or great one. Its logic is the logic of events—its figures those of the arithmetic. This process may make a strong speech, but it does not produce oratory. Its appeals are to prejudice. Even its pretense is offensive. It is marred by sneers and sarcasms, and, while these may please enthusiastic admirers, they were never known to persuade men into the speaker's way of thinking. So great, indeed, is Senator Conkling's characteristic failing in this direction, that he could apparently hardly wait to get through with his stilted exordium before dropping the gall of his venom upon President Hayes. We are surprised that this passage was not hissed. It would have been if delivered by anybody but the 'imperious' Senator, in the 'imperial' city of New York."

The Herald continues:

Coming to the issues of the campaign, Senator Conkling really presents but one, though he gives to it many turns and twists. And this issue is, whether the Democratic party deserves to be intrusted with uncontrolled power in the nation. Speaking to this question, nothing is more natural than that he should consider its record for the past dozen or twenty years, and this of course he finds no difficulty in painting very dark, for the Democrats themselves, by their series of what we have denominated blunders that are worse than crimes, and crimes that are worse than blunders, have furnished him plenty of dark material. When, however, he accepts the Southern or sectional phase of this issue, with mock regret, wishing it were not so, but saying that it is—and that in twelve states "there is no free debate, no equal rights"—he knows that he is not telling the truth. Before the great meeting at Blackville, S. C., early in the summer, the Republican organs were very sure that no such gatherings would be permitted, and the impossibility of free discussions was urged as a reason for abandoning a canvass of the South.— When, however, it transpired that the meeting was not disturbed, they changed their tune, and said a canvass would not amount to anything, as there would be cheating in the count. The canvass of the South was deliberately abandoned, in order that that the managers might treat "the solid South" as so much funded capital for use at the North, and not, as Senator Conkling declares, because free debate was impossible. The power of the South in the Democratic party and the danger to the settlements of the war constitute the burden of his speech. But has not the South the right to vote as it pleases—provided, always, that it does so freely and fairly? Or does the Senator propose that "the Southern question" shall be kept alive until the South joins a party which has abandoned its organization in most of their States, or until the Democratic party will agree to die and be buried? When is this indictment, bad as we concede it to be, to run out? Will the North and West probably pay any less proportion of the taxes for the next dozen years? Under what conditions will he agree that the Republican party is no longer essential to the preservation of the government, and is the heaven-ordained ruler of the country? The whole argument of his speech would make the dynasty perpetual.

and prefer to hold them and pay cash for American produce. Yesterday $500,000 in bullion was withdrawn from the Bank of England for shipment to this country, and the German steamer Gollert brings from Hamburg $1,875,000 in specie, and from Havre $1,000,000.

A young woman of Blooming Prairie, Minn., has confessed to strangling her illegitimate child near Osage, Ia., last May. She has been arrested, and will probably be held for murder.

The fast newspaper train from New York for Long Branch collided with a train of empty passenger cars near the Long Branch station yesterday morning. The side of one car of the news train was torn away and two other cars were wrecked. Three young men were severely injured, one of whom, Jeremiah Culliland, is in a critical condition. The disaster is ascribed to the carelessness of John Erickson, engineer.

At Pleasant Hill, Mo., on Saturday night, William and Robert Van Holtz, brothers, while buying provisions in the store of Henry Stock, were ordered out by Stock, who, at the same moment fired a pistol at them. They returned the fire killing Stock and severely wounding another man, named Alexander, and then surrendered themselves to the police.

The house of Martin Weinrich, on the line between Dane and Columbia counties, in Wisconsin, was discovered on fire last Sunday night. The door being forced, the bodies of Weinrich and his wife, bearing fatal shot wounds, were found within. The couple had lived unhappily, and it is supposed Weinrich shot his wife and then committed suicide.

Frank Stillwell was shot dead by George Glass on Saturday night while attempting to force an entrance into the latter's house, a disreputable place in Urbana, Ill. Stillwell had been drinking. He leaves a wife and child.

Thomas Smith and Wesley Thomas, negroes, quarrelled in Burlingame, Kansas, on Sunday night, and Thomas was killed. A second shot, fired by Smith, passed through the window of a saloon and mortally wounded a man named Baker.

Michael Wood was arrested in the act of setting fire to a building in College Point, L. I., last Saturday night. Seven incendiary fires have lately occurred in this place, and it is believed that all can be traced to him.

John Dismen was found dead on the stoop of his house at Red Bank, N. J., yesterday morning. While helplessly drunk he had fallen flat on his face with his arms beneath him, and been smothered to death. He was 45 years of age.

The report of the robbery on a Third avenue car in New York is contradicted by the police of that city. They say the affair was nothing more than a disturbance made by two drunken men, who refused to pay their fare to the conductor.

The quarterly interest on the four- and a half per cent. loan, due September 1st, will aggregate $2,800,000. Checks for the payment of the interest on the registered bonds will be sent out by the U. S. Treasurer in a few days.

Mrs. Moles, aged 50 years, was found hanging to a tree near Wheeling, W. Va., on Saturday night. It is supposed she committed suicide to escape "family jars."

The trial at Deadwood of R. O. Adams, for embezzling nearly $12,000, has resulted in his conviction. It is thought he will give bail and appeal the case to the Territorial Supreme Court.

J. C. Miller, one of the proprietors of the Daily Critic, in Washington, D. C., was severely if not fatally injured yesterday, by falling from a third-story window.

Joseph Willner, aged 55 years, committed suicide in Troy, N. Y., on Sunday morning. He has been suffering from sickness, which, it was supposed, had effected his mind.

A telegram from Montrose, Pa., says Warren has been convicted of murder in the second degree. The jury were out thirty-nine hours.

A jewelry store in Danbury, Conn., was robbed of about $500 worth of property by three burglars a few nights ago.

General Albert J. Myer, chief of the Signal Service, remains in a precarious condition at Buffalo. His death was momentarily expected last night.

The condition of Washington McLean, sick at Long Branch, was further improved yesterday, but is still considered critical.

Alfred Terry, colored, was shot dead by James Thorp, in a quarrel, at Kansas City, on Sunday.

John Smithwrite, fireman on the propeller Canistor, was fatally shot by Francis Trainor, in Buffalo, last night. Trainor escaped.

BURLINGAME'S BLOODY BOOM.
A Double Shooting in Osage County.
Mr. A. S. Houck, of this city, who returned from a trip over the eastern end of the Cottonwood division of the Santa Fe road, Monday, gives the following particulars of a tragedy which occurred at Burlingame Saturday night:
Mr. Houck says as the train pulled into Burlingame Sunday, his attention was attracted by a very large and excited crowd which gathered around the depot, and presently Sheriff Smith, of Osage county, marched into the car, having in charge Thomas Smith, a colored man, manacled and handcuffed, being under arrest for the double shooting of Bob Thomas and Logue Baker, both citizens of Burlingame. By permission of the Sheriff Mr. Houck was permitted to interview the prisoner, who told him that Thomas had accused him of being too intimate with his wife, and threatened to shoot him for inducing her to leave him. Smith denied the charge, but on Saturday evening, as he was coming out of Baker's saloon where he had gone to get a drink, he met Thomas, who, he said, came towards him with a pistol in his hand. Smith told him to hold up his hand or he would shoot him, and Thomas refusing to obey, Smith shot him in the stomach and subsequently struck him with his revolver, which went off, wounding Smith in the hand, and discharging a ball which passed through the window wounding Baker, the saloonist, who is expected to die. Thomas walked several squares, but soon after expired. After the shooting, Smith gave himself up, and for a while there were loud threats of lynching him, some of the citizens even going so far as to procure a rope. The murderer was in the employ of Wibley & Henson, of this city, three years ago, and was pretty well known in Emporia. He claims to have shot Thomas in self-defence and expressed great regret over the accident which resulted in the shooting of Baker, with whom he was very friendly. The latter was still alive at 2 o'clock this morning, but is not expect ed to recover.

MONTENEGRO is desirous of Servian support, and has sent an agent to the Servian Government requesting it.

CONGRESSMAN PAGE was renominated Wednesday evening by the Republicans of the Second California District.

ENGLISH troops are being poured into Ireland daily to awe the rebellious people of that country into submission if not loyalty.

CONGRESSMAN CANNON addressed a large and enthusiastic Republican gathering at Decatur last evening on the issues of the campaign.

THE Universalist Church at Marblehead, Mass., was burned by incendiarles yesterday morning. The loss was $25,000. The insurance is placed at $4,000.

THE Canadians residing in the vicinity of Sarnia are considerably excited over the recent discovery of silver of great purity at Silver Islet, near that place.

SENATOR ALLISON and Congressman Updegrault opened the Republican campaign in Iowa at Dubuque last night. A large audience turned out to hear them.

In yesterday's ball games for the League championship, Providence, Cleveland, Troy, and Cincinnati were victorious against Chicago, Worcester, Buffalo, and Boston.

The Macedonian Bulgarians have sent an address to the Prince of Bulgaria, expressing a desire to become his subjects. The Prince, it is said, encouraged the petitionors.

The Greek volunteer force is being rapidly organized at Athens. Camps have been formed near the city, and the recruits are drilled daily in the public streets.

A fire at Sherlock's Mills, N. Y., yesterday, destroyed Mr. Sherlock's steam-mill and twenty dwellings. The loss is very heavy. Thoro was about $40,000 insurance on the buildings.

Mr. J. Stovail, was nominated for Congress yesterday by the Roadjustors of the Fifth Virginia District. The district is now represented by the Hon. George C. Caboll, Democrat.

CHARLES H. TARDY, President of the Colored Relief Board of St. Louis, has advised that 10,000 negroes will emigrate from Mississippi and Louisiana within the next two months for Kansas and other Western States.

After a very spirited contest the Hon. Ezra B. Taylor, of Trumbull County, was nominated for Congress by the Republicans of the Nineteenth Ohio (Garfield's) District. The nomination gives much satisfaction.

A GENERAL rising has taken place in the Mexican Provinces of Sonora, Sinaloa, and Jalisco against Gen. Gonzales, President-elect of the Mexican Republic. The leaders in this last rebellion are Gen. Canto and Gen. Marquez.

ADMIRAL RINQUET, the pro-Bonapartist naval officer in command at Cherbourg, attended the banquet given to President Orvvy, Leon Say, and Gambetta yesterday. On leaving the banquet he was violently hooted by a mob.

ROGER RUSSEL, an old man of 70, fired two barrels of a shotgun into the face and breast of his son-in-law, John Norman, four miles from New Albany, Ind., last evening, inflicting fatal wounds. Norman had been ill-troubling his wife, Russel's daughter.

PRESIDENT HAYES left Columbus last evening for Washington. He remarked before leaving that the Reunion was the largest he ever attended. He complimented the people on the general good conduct which characterized all the proceedings.

JUNGE J. D. THOMAN was nominated for Congress yesterday by the Democrats of the Seventeenth Ohio District. Con. Banning was nominated in the First, the Hon. Samuel Hunt in the Second, and Congressman Hurd in the Sixth District by the same party.

The Tennessee Debt-Repudiators adopted a platform yesterday denouncing the State-Credit party as being in league with railroad and banking corporations, as machine-politicians who represent only a caucus clique, and as a party attempting to defraud the taxpayers of the State. They then proceeded to endorse the Cincinnati platform, except the plank referring to the State and National credit. The platform

favors a liberal support of the public schools and opposes competition between convict and free labor.

The reunion of the veterans of Central Illinois at Springfield yesterday was an affair of great interest to the old soldiers participating and to the large number of spectators present. There were excellent speeches by Gov. Cullom, Gen. Palmer, and ox-Gov. Oglesby.

The existence of an unholy alliance between the Democrats and Greenbackers in Maine received further confirmation yesterday. A party named Fogg, who received the Democratic nomination for Congress from the Second District of that State, was indorsed by the Greenbackers.

A freight-train on the St. Paul & Duluth Railway was thrown off the track near Pino City yesterday morning by a broken rail. Nine cars were completely wrecked. Three Minneapolis boys, named Peter Martin, John Ervino, and George Adams, who were stealing rides on the train, were killed.

Free Speech North and South
The Natchez (Miss.) Democrat gives quite a little essay upon the right of free speech as exercised, not in the South alone, but at the North and in England. It finds fault with a "new kink," which it says "the John Lynch radicals," have devised, which is "to get up political meetings under the name of colored picnics and then turn them into political meetings." "The plan," it says, "is to attach to them simply the idea of social assemblages, and thus ensure the absence of any but radical white men," and goes on to describe one of these meetings, gotten up ostensibly as a picnic, but really for the dangerous purpose of disseminating radical doctrines. Mr. Lynch and a party named Harris were present at the meeting, and made radical speeches, but it seemed that they were not to be left to the enjoyment of their own meeting, but one Cox, a colored Democrat, a warm friend of General Chalmers, had smuggled himself in and insisted upon replying to the radical speeches. He was told by "the Lynch strikers" that they did not want to hear any Democrat, and the account says, "Cox would doubtless have been hooted down had it not been for the efforts of white men on the ground," who seemed to be conveniently on hand. "If the majority of the audience had been Democrats," says this Bourbon organ, "and had interrupted Lynch's speech, we have no doubt that letters would have gone to his friends in the Northern States giving the most exaggerated accounts of 'the outrage,' and howling about free speech being denied him in the South. Nothing gratifies radicals like John Lynch more than conveying to his Northern friends the idea that the Democracy of his own State, the intelligent people from whom his own race must naturally expect elevation and education, are a set of ruffians and bull dozers, and a far inferior people to his Northern friends. Lynch and his friends could not expect that they would be allowed to utter these or any other false and injurious statements before an audience when the abused class are present, without interruption." This then is the Southern idea of a political campaign; that Republicans at least are not to be permitted to make speeches in exposition of theis own and their opponents' political views, without having some of their opponents present to answer their arguments on the spot, whether they desire to hear or not. But this partisan philosopher, the editor of the Democrat, goes on and elaborates his ideas of free speech in a way that will strike the Northern reader as somewhat peculiar. He says:

And in this connection we will say, in reply to the charge that free speech is not allowed in the south, that free speech is not tolerated to an in jurious extent in any country. The right of expressing an opinion belongs equally as much to an audience as it does to the speaker. If sentiments are uttered which do not meet the approval of an audience, they have the same right to express their disapproval as the speaker has to utter the obnoxious sentiments. This is done far more in the north than in the south, and more in England than it is in America. Let an actor say something which is disagreeable to his audience and he is hissed off the stage, or if a public speaker does not reflect the views of his hearers he is hooted down and sometimes even pelted off. A public speaker must take his chance of being listened to respectfully, and he may rest assured, in any country, that if he antagonizes the views of his audience he will hear expressions of their disapproval. If J. L. Lynch's crowd on Ship Island had been strong enough, Mr. Cox would never have had an opportunity to speak. If the opposition to Democracy had been as strong as Lynch would have it, no Democratic speaker would have a hearing. But for unearly Lynch does not have the influence once wielded by Dave Young in Concordia parish, or he, as Dave did on one memorable occasion, would have called on his votaries to "follow Hanner," and would have left his opponent to talk to vacant space. These old time tricks must be watched by the Democracy and sternly rebuked.

The idea that free speech is not tolerated to "an injurious extent" in any country, is a nice distinction. Who are to be the judges as to whether the free speech is injurious, and what remedies are to be applied? Plainly it is to be left to the Southern Democracy to decide what shall be tolerated in the way of free speech in that section of the country, and the remedies are to be the raising of an uproar, the playing of bands, etc., to drown out the free speech, as was done in Alabama, or the forced presence of some one to insist upon answering the arguments contained in free speeches. It would not do to let the poison go out unaccompanied by the antidote. The givngs out of this Bourbon organ are only confirmatory of what the Republican press has all along claimed, that there is really no freedom of opinion in very many portions of the South, and that the whole policy is to suppress the utterance of any political doctrines which do not square with Democratic ideas. Political intolerance is the reigning idea, and it crops out in every movement from mob violence and murder, down to social ostracism and neighborhood persecution. There is no freedom there such as is enjoyed in the North. Whoever opposes the dominant political sentiment, does so at his peril.
